analysis.one_liner: Replaces income taxes with a flat 10% tax on wages while repealing corporate, estate, and investment-income taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced January 4, 1995 with 5 cosponsors, it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and died there when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have eliminated the corporate income tax, the estate tax, and the gift tax entirely, and wiped out every deduction, exclusion, and credit in the individual income tax code. In their place, it would have taxed only wages and self-employment earnings, at a flat 10% above a $10,000 exemption. Interest, dividends, capital gains, rents, and pensions would be taxed at nothing. It also would have forgiven all income tax debts and penalties for years before 1994.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations and their shareholders would stop paying federal income tax altogether. Wealthy households would pay no tax on interest, dividends, capital gains, or rents, since only wages and self-employment earnings count as taxable income under the bill. Estates and gifts would pass free of federal tax. Anyone with unpaid income taxes from before 1994 would have the debt and penalties forgiven.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the corporate income tax, the corporate alternative minimum tax, and taxes on insurance companies, investment companies, real estate investment trusts, and foreign corporations' U.S. income.
Taxes only 'earned income' — wages, salaries, and self-employment net earnings — at 10% above a $10,000 exemption, leaving interest, dividends, capital gains, and rental income untaxed.
Repeals the estate tax, the gift tax, and the generation-skipping transfer tax, so large inheritances would pass tax-free.
Declares amnesty for all income tax liability, penalties, and interest for taxable years before 1994.
Exempts the first $10,000 of earnings (adjusted for inflation), plus tips and pension or annuity income, from the new 10% tax.

analysis.who_pays: Wage earners and the self-employed would bear essentially the entire federal income tax burden. They would lose every deduction and credit — the earned income credit, child credits, mortgage interest, charitable deductions, retirement account exclusions — and pay 10% on every dollar of wages above $10,000, while investment income went untaxed. The forgone corporate and estate tax revenue would have to be made up somewhere, through other taxes or borrowing.

drawbacks.text: The bill strikes all individual deductions, exclusions, and credits, which would eliminate the earned income credit, child-related tax benefits, the mortgage interest deduction, and charitable deductions in one stroke.

Because only earned income is taxed, a worker making $60,000 in wages pays the tax while someone living entirely off interest, dividends, and capital gains pays nothing — a structural shift of the tax burden from wealth to work.
Pension and annuity income is exempt, so retirees would pay no income tax while current workers pay for the same government.
The blanket amnesty would wipe out unpaid income taxes, penalties, and interest owed for any year before 1994, rewarding those who never paid.

Eliminating the corporate tax, estate tax, and gift tax while cutting the individual rate to a flat 10% would remove enormous amounts of federal revenue with no replacement funding mechanism in the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow almost entirely one way: to corporations, investors, and heirs, paid for by wage earners who lose every deduction and credit and keep paying tax on all their income while investment income goes free. The one genuine relief for working people — a $10,000 tax-free threshold and a low flat rate — is overwhelmed by the loss of credits and deductions and by the shift of the whole burden onto labor. The pre-1994 amnesty is a further giveaway with no public-side payoff.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Philip Crane introduced the Crane Tithe Tax Act of 1995 in the House on January 4, 1995.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and no further action was ever taken on it.
Five House Republicans cosponsored the bill.
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, workers kept the existing tax code with its deductions and credits, and corporations, investors, and large estates continued to pay federal income, corporate, and estate taxes as before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wage earners and the current tax code

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 4, 1995 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Rep. Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the 104th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only recorded support was the Republican sponsor and his five Republican cosponsors.

industries.note: The bill repeals every corporate-level federal income tax, including the corporate minimum tax, ending corporate tax liability entirely. The revenue would otherwise fund services that wage earners would continue to be taxed for.

Investment income — interest, dividends, capital gains, rents — would be taxed at zero because only earned income counts, and the estate and gift taxes would disappear. The pre-1994 amnesty would also erase any unpaid tax debts.
Special taxes on life insurance companies, mutual insurance companies, regulated investment companies, and real estate investment trusts would be repealed outright.
